rows.answer: He rushed at her with the axe; her mouth twitched piteously, as one sees babies’ mouths, when they begin to be frightened, stare intently at what frightens them and are on the point of screaming. And that hapless Lizaveta was so simple and had been so thoroughly crushed and scared that she did not even raise a hand to guard her face, though that was the most necessary and natural action at the moment, for the axe was raised over her face. She only put up her empty left hand, but not to her face, slowly holding it out before her as though motioning him away. The axe fell with the sharp edge just on the skull and split at one blow all the top of the head. She fell heavily at once.

I cannot recall whether Raskolnikov breaks down and confesses the murder to Sonia, for the recollections do not extend to that moment. We see him stand in hesitation at her door, asking himself the strange question of whether he must tell her who killed Lizaveta, feeling already the agonizing sense of his impotence before the inevitable, but the page turns and the confession itself is not given to us.

Yes, he knelt down in the middle of that square, bowed down to the earth, and kissed that filthy earth with bliss and rapture, getting up only to bow down a second time, while the crowd around him laughed and thought him merely drunk, with a youth observing that he was boozed and a workman adding that he was going to Jerusalem and saying good-bye to his children and his country. And it was then, upon that very second bowing down in the Hay Market, that he saw Sonia standing fifty paces from him, hiding behind one of the wooden shanties, having followed him on his painful way, so that he felt and knew once for all that she was with him for ever and would follow him to the ends of the earth wherever fate might take him, which wrung his heart even as he reached the fatal place and went resolutely into the yard to mount to the third storey, feeling as though the fateful moment was still far off and that he had plenty of time left for consideration, while his legs were numb and gave way under him upon those same spiral stairs littered with rubbish and eggshells, past the same open doors and the same kitchens with their fumes and stench, returning to the very place he had not visited since that day.

He showed Dounia two empty rooms to let, unlocking a door that led directly from his bedroom, so that he might explain how he had sat there listening on two successive evenings, for two hours each time, to Sofya Semyonovna’s table where she sat talking to Rodion Romanovitch, using a chair brought from his rooms by that locked door to listen more conveniently. He then brought Avdotya Romanovna back into his sitting-room and offered her a chair at least seven feet from her, and though there was probably the same glow in his eyes which had once frightened Dounia so much, and though she shuddered and looked about her distrustfully because the secluded position of his lodging had suddenly struck her, she had laid his letter on the table, demanding that he speak and prove the hints he had written regarding her brother's crime, saying she did not believe a word of it and that it was a disgusting and ridiculous suspicion.

I cannot recall whether she reads it to him, though I remember well enough that when she asked him if he believed in Lazarus’ rising from the dead, he answered firmly, literally, that he did. Whether the actual reading is set down between us in those pages—of that I am no longer certain, and I will not invent what has slipped from my memory into the dark.

The Grand Inquisitor comes in the pitch darkness of the breathless night of Seville, with a light in his hand, to the close, gloomy vaulted prison where the Prisoner has been shut after being recognized by the people on the hot pavements and led away. He stands in the doorway, gazing into His face for a minute or two, and then asks if it is truly He, yet instantly bids Him be silent, saying He has no right to add anything to what was said of old, and declaring that on the morrow he will condemn Him and burn Him at the stake as the worst of heretics while the very people who kissed His feet will rush to heap up the embers at a single sign.

Yes, that is precisely the burden of his rebellion, though he states it with a tortured, Euclidian understanding, declaring himself a bug who cannot comprehend why the world is arranged as it is, where cause follows effect simply and directly yet leaves him with no guilt to assign and no comfort in some remote, infinite time and space. He tells his brother that he must have justice here on earth, and that he could see it himself, or else he will destroy himself; and it is specifically the tears of innocent children—the tortured babes crying out to "dear, kind God" with their little unavenged fists in the dark—that he uses to make his case clear, returning the ticket of admission to this higher harmony because the cost is too monstrous, filled with the innocent blood of creatures who have not yet eaten of the apple and cannot be held to blame.

There was indeed a terrible, almost indecent haste in the way that decomposition manifested itself in the body of Father Zossima, so swiftly that not even a single day had passed before the signs appeared, and this physical fact became a weapon in the hands of those who had long harbored a deeply-rooted hostility toward the institution of elders as a pernicious innovation. Is it not strange how the human heart—even within holy walls, among men who have ostensibly renounced the world—latches upon the corruption of another with such malicious delight? For while the elder had lived, winning hearts more by love than by miracles, his very saintliness had bred a silent, accumulating jealousy, so that when the fragrance of sanctity was replaced so abruptly by the unmistakable smell of decay, many could not conceal the triumph gleaming in their malignant eyes, as if the physical putrefaction of a man’s mortal frame could somehow disprove the beauty of the soul that had inhabited it, while even those who had loved him were strangely mortified and affronted, as though God Himself had suddenly permitted the minority of bitter, secret enemies to get the upper hand.

Lizabetha Prokofievna was indeed driven beside herself, viewing the whole affair as one huge, fantastical, absurd, and unpardonable mistake, crying out in her indignation that the prince was an idiot and a fool who knew nothing of the world and had no place in it, asking whom he could possibly be shown to or what old Bielokonski would say, because they had never thought of such a husband as that for their Aglaya, yet even as her maternal heart trembled with this anger, there rose within her another voice—a troubling, contradictory voice—that whispered: "And *why* is not the prince such a husband as you would have desired for Aglaya?"—and it was this very voice that annoyed her above all else, driving her to worry and foresee everything while the rest of the household sat silent.

Yes, it was precisely that, his return to Russia after spending more than four years abroad for his health, suffering from that strange nervous malady, a kind of epilepsy with convulsive spasms, having been kept at the expense of a Swiss doctor who even gave him money for his journey when Mr. Pavlicheff, who had been supporting him there, died, and writing to Mrs. General Epanchin who did not answer his letter, so that he came back with his whole set-up in a bundle, knowing scarcely where he was going to stay, and sitting opposite those passengers in the railway carriage who laughed at him—yes, that very impoverished return, laden with the torment of his affliction.

Yes, they gather there, and Liputin meets Erkel and Shatov at the entrance to the grotto, where Shatov does not bow or offer his hand but at once speaks of the spade and another lantern, stamping with his foot ten paces from the end of the grotto towards the wood; and at that moment Tolkatchenko rushes out from behind a tree and springs at him from behind, while Erkel seizes him by the elbows and Liputin attacks him from the front, knocking him down and pinning him to the ground, at which point Pyotr Stepanovitch darts up with his revolver, which Shatov recognizes before a short and desperate scream is cut off as Pyotr Stepanovitch firmly and accurately puts the revolver to his forehead, presses it to it, and pulls the trigger, producing a shot that is not loud, while Shigalov, scarcely three paces away, hears the shout and the shot but does not turn or even stop, and death is almost instantaneous, and Pyotr Stepanovitch, the only one who preserves all his faculties though perhaps not quite cool, squats on his heels and searches the murdered man's pockets hastily.

Yulia Mihailovna is indeed engaged in the organizing of a grand fête, intended for the benefit of the governesses of our province, and she is surrounded by her chosen circle, though we must look closer at the strange quality of that devotion. 

She has bustling constantly around her Pyotr Stepanovitch, and that little clerk Lyamshin, who once visited Stepan Trofimovitch and now finds favour through his piano-playing and running of errands, alongside Liputin, whom she destines to be the editor of a new independent provincial paper. There are various ladies, married and single, and Karmazinov too, who announces aloud with a complacent air that he will agreeably astonish everyone when the literary quadrille begins, while an extraordinary multitude of donors and subscribers turn up from the select society of the town, and even the unselect if they produce the cash, for Yulia Mihailovna observes that sometimes it is a positive duty to allow the mixing of classes, asking, "for otherwise who is to enlighten them?" 

A private drawing-room committee is formed to decide that the fête shall be of a democratic character, and the enormous list of subscriptions tempts them to lavish expenditure upon a marvellous scale, which is why it is put off several times, as they debate whether the ball is to take place in the immense house belonging to the marshal's wife or at Varvara Petrovna's mansion at Skvoreshniki. Varvara Petrovna herself would dearly have liked it in her own house, and it is singular how this proud woman almost makes up to Yulia Mihailovna, perhaps because Yulia Mihailovna in her turn seems almost fawning upon Nikolay Vsyevolodovitch and is more gracious to him than to anyone, while Pyotr Stepanovitch continually whispers to strengthen ideas in the governor's household. 

Within this intimate circle surrounding her, particularly among the younger members, it is considered admissible to play all sorts of pranks, sometimes rather free-and-easy ones, becoming a principle among them as they arrange picnics and parties, go about the town in a cavalcade in carriages and on horseback, and seek out adventures simply for the sake of having an amusing story to tell, treating our town as though it were a sort of Glupov and earning the name of the jeerers or sneerers because they do not stick at anything. Yet for all her belief that she is surrounded by followers who are fanatically devoted to her, up to the last hour before the fête takes place, she remains blind to the state of public feeling, unaware of the bewildered, strained cynicism predominant in everyone, and unconscious of how turbulent times of upheaval always bring the riff-raff to the surface—those who are without any aim or symptom of an idea, yet rise to the top and fall under the control of others.

Virginsky does not stop it, no, though he is caught in that terrible fever of the mind which accompanies such dark deeds, running round beforehand to persuade himself that Shatov will not be harmed because his wife has returned and given birth to a child, as if human nature could be so easily measured by arithmetic or safe conclusions. And then, when it is done, when the stones have been tied on and the body lies there in the gloom of those huge ancient pines by the Crown wood, it is Virginsky who begins faintly shuddering all over, clasping his hands and crying out bitterly at the top of his voice that "It's not the right thing, it's not, it's not at all!" Yet he cries out only *afterwards*, when the deed is accomplished and the horror has taken its visible shape, just as Lyamshin shrieks with that animal terror and buries himself in a frenzy, proving how these men who enter into such conspiracies with a lightness of heart are utterly crushed and broken when the actual blood is spilled and the awful reality stands revealed before them.

Yes, it is indeed true, and one may trace the very contours of that strange, delicate existence, for he flung himself into the arms of her passionate sympathy and classic friendship, and his position under her patronage was settled for more than twenty years. Yet what a paradox lies in such a shelter! To be bound for decades to a grand estate like Skvoreshniki, living in the shadow of a magnificent and imperious protector—Varvara Petrovna, who watched over him, defended him, and yet held him fast within the orbit of her formidable will. Was it peace he found there, or a kind of gilded captivity? He was a man who fancied himself soaring on eagle wings, attempting lectures and researching Spanish history, or perhaps pondering the Dresden Madonna, and yet he remained ever dependent, ever caught between the high-flown phrases of an earlier generation and the perplexing, restless pressure of the young people rising up around them. Twenty years! Think of the length of it, the quiet erosion of actual independence, the daily accommodation to another's greatness, until the very air of that patronage became the only world he knew, even as the ground beneath them all began so fearfully to shift.

It was not merely sport, no, but the exercise of my skill that carried me away, speaking stiffly, artificially, even bookishly, because I could not speak except like a book, though I knew and felt that I should be understood. And having attained my effect, I was suddenly panic-stricken, witnessing such despair as I had never seen before, her youthful body shuddering all over as though in convulsions, biting her hand till it bled, thrusting her fingers into her dishevelled hair. Yet when she had gone and left behind her that crumpled blue five-rouble note on the table—the very one I had thrust into her hand a minute before—I could not endure it, for I was such an egoist and so lacking in respect for my fellow-creatures that I could not even imagine she would do so, and I flew like a madman to dress, flinging on what I could at random and running headlong after her into the still night where the snow was coming down in masses.

The mass of mankind is divided by a certain law into two categories: the ordinary and the extraordinary. The first, the ordinary, must serve only as material, being conservative by nature, obedient, living in subjection, and having no right to transgress the law. The second, the extraordinary, have a right to commit crimes and to transgress the law in various ways, simply because they are extraordinary, because they are men of the future who move the world and lead it to its goal, even if that goal requires stepping over corpses or eliminating obstacles. They have the right to permit their conscience to step over certain obstacles, should the realization of their ideas—which may perhaps save all humanity—demand it.

Ah, but to arrest him straightway—what does that actually accomplish? A man like that, you see, a man caught in the terrible web of his own dark theory, cannot simply be taken by the collar like a common thief and locked away in a cell without something far worse happening within his spirit. If you only put him under lock and key, he remains convinced of his own mathematical grandeur, he shuts himself up in his pride, he nurses his wounds and curses the mere clumsiness of his execution rather than the monstrousness of the deed itself. No, he must break down from the inside; he must come to see the utter falsehood of his intellectual tower through the agonizing pressure of his own conscience, until he understands that he is not some extraordinary creature permitted to step over blood, but simply a weak, suffering human being who has crushed his own soul. Porfiry Petrovitch understands this deeply—he is an investigator of a very peculiar sort, a psychologist who knows that a man must be brought to the point where he cannot bear his own isolation any longer. The poor wretch must be made to feel the full weight of his separation from mankind, because it is only through that terrible, suffering realization, through the desperate need for human air and a living truth, that he can ever be led to a genuine surrender and the possibility of a resurrection. Otherwise, you have only captured a body while the soul remains defiant, snarling in the dark, untouched and unrepentant.

An elegant carriage stood in the middle of the road with a pair of spirited grey horses, while the coachman had got off his box and stood by, holding the horses by the bridle, as a mass of people gathered round with the police standing in front, one of whom held a lighted lantern turning it on something lying close to the wheels. On the ground a man who had been run over lay apparently unconscious and covered with blood; he was very badly dressed, but not like a workman, with blood flowing from his head and face, and his face crushed, mutilated, and disfigured, so that he was evidently badly injured. The coachman kept wailing, asking what more he could do if he had not been driving fast or shouting to him, declaring he was going quietly and not in a hurry, and that everyone could see him going along just like everybody else, because a drunk man can't walk straight as we all know. He said he saw him crossing the street, staggering and almost falling, and that he had shouted a first and a second and a third time, then held the horses in, but the man fell straight under their feet either on purpose or because he was very tipsy, and the young horses started and made things worse when he screamed. A voice in the crowd confirmed that the coachman had indeed shouted three times, and another and a third agreed they all heard it, while the coachman remained not very much distressed and frightened because the carriage belonged to a rich and important person awaiting it somewhere, and the police were in no little anxiety to avoid upsetting his arrangements, having only to take the injured man to the police station and the hospital, while no one knew his name, and meanwhile Raskolnikov pushed his way in as far as he could to see.

I must confess that I cannot recall the entirety of such a disastrous literary fête in the precise manner you describe it, for my memory is burdened by so many other agonizing scenes, yet I remember well enough the strange, feverish atmosphere from which such catastrophes are born among us. There was a fête arranged with such boundless, pitiful hopes—imagined by poor Yulia Mihailovna as a brilliant triumph of enlightened thought, complete with a literary matinée, a ball, rumours of princes with lorgnettes, stewards with rosettes, and even the promise of "honest Russian thought" dancing in costume. She was so blind to the actual state of public feeling, so persuaded that she was surrounded by fanatically devoted followers, right up to the very hour when the whole wretched business unraveled. 

And why should it not unraveled? Every Russian, you see, is inordinately delighted at any public scandal and disorder, feeling a deep, implacable resentment and a forced, bewildered cynicism towards everything. In such turbulent times of transition, this low riff-raff always rises to the surface—creatures without an aim or even a symptom of an idea, merely doing their utmost to give expression to uneasiness and impatience, though they unconsciously fall under the control of the little group of advanced people who are always in a hurry to be ahead of everyone else. The programme itself carried the very germs of disorder, not least because the public was possessed by the disastrous rumour of a free luncheon accompanied by champagne, reasoning that since the tickets cost three roubles, food simply had to be provided. It is all so painfully familiar—this frantic reaching after some grand, brilliant exhibition of culture and intellect that inevitably turns into a spectacle of our own most ridiculous and shameful humiliations.

It is done because in that simple, almost childlike act—taking off a tin cross and giving it in exchange for another’s gold one—there is an instinctive reach for brotherhood, as if by such an outward sign two men, standing at opposite poles of the human spirit, might bind themselves together and cast out the dark distrust that lingers between them. And yet, even as the exchange is made, the bitter, ironical smile does not altogether leave the newly-adopted brother’s face, and the look of suspicion remains. What does it actually mean? It means a terrible, unbreakable bond forged in the shadow of mutual guilt and impending doom, where they are brothers not merely by the cross upon the breast, but by the knife held and the knife contemplated, so that whether the hand is stayed or whether it strikes, they are mutually guilty in the sight of one another, bound by a jealousy so fierce and a darkness so absolute that even the grace of an angel could not undo it.

I remember that room, and the terrible stillness that fell upon it, as if men had suddenly forgotten how to breathe, standing there in their evening clothes and white gloves, watching a fortune smoulder. She stood by the fire and waited, with her intent gaze fixed upon him—upon Gania, who stood speechless and motionless, his hands folded, a silly, meaningless smile playing on his white, death-like lips. He could not take his eyes off the packet, and a hundred thousand roubles lay there, turning to ash. 

She had told him to pull it out, mocking him with the fire, daring him to plunge his fingers into the burning logs for the money. And everyone gasped, and some even crossed themselves, whispering among themselves, *“She’s mad—she’s mad!”* while others, like Ptitsin and Totski, turned as white as their handkerchiefs, unable to tear their eyes from the flames. Gania did not move; a new trial had come to birth in his soul, and it was evident to all that he did not intend to rescue the money, though he knew he might hang himself afterwards out of despair. 

And then the fire, which had been choked for a moment, caught the paper from below, mounted the sides, and burst fully into flames, drawing forth cries of woe and horror from every corner of the room. Amidst this madness, Rogojin stood in the seventh heaven of delight, his whole being concentrated in one rapturous gaze of ecstasy, drinking her in and yelling to the blackguards about him, *“That’s the sort of woman for me! Which of you would think of doing a thing like that?”* while the prince watched the whole scene, silent and dejected.

Because man is not a piano-key, not a stop on an organ pipe, not a mere note played upon by the laws of nature and arithmetic, where everything can be calculated and tabulated so that soon one will be able to desire nothing except by the calendar. Shower upon him every earthly blessing, drown him in a sea of happiness, give him such economic prosperity that he has nothing else to do but sleep, eat cakes, and busy himself with the continuation of his species—and even then, out of sheer ingratitude, sheer spite, man will play you some nasty trick. He will deliberately desire the most fatal rubbish, the most uneconomical absurdity, simply to introduce into all that positive good sense his fatal fantastic element. It is his vulgar folly and his fantastic dreams that he desires to retain, simply in order to prove to himself that men still are men and not the keys of a piano. 

What sort of free will is left when we come to tabulation and arithmetic, when it will all be a case of twice two makes four? Twice two makes four without our will, and as if free will meant that! Even if man were nothing but a piano-key, even if this were proved to him by natural science and mathematics, he would not become reasonable. He would purposely do something perverse out of simple ingratitude, simply to gain his point, and if he finds no other means he will contrive destruction and chaos, will contrive sufferings of all sorts, only to prove to himself every minute that he is a man and not a piano-key. And if it should be that all this too—chaos and darkness and curses—could be calculated and tabulated beforehand, then man would purposely go mad in order to be rid of reason and gain his point, risking his skin, perhaps even at the cost of cannibalism, just to convince himself that he is a man and not a note in an instrument.

I cannot recall how that farewell dinner party ended up going wrong for the narrator. My memory does not stretch to that particular evening, for my thoughts were elsewhere, dwelling upon the strange, contradictory depths of the human soul—upon those moments when a man, full of wine and the agonizing, burning desire to justify himself, speaks of charity, of a civil general visiting the wretched exiles upon the Vorobeef Hills, and of the profound, terrible need we all have to feel that we have done some small good in this dark world. Beyond the crossing of the Nicolai bridge and the boasting of a good action, the recollections fade, and I cannot say what failure or discord awaited them at the end.

Zverkov plays the part of one of those fortunate, stupid creatures of nature, favored by gifts, self-confident, and radiant in their unquestioned rightness, before whom we all instinctively grovel simply because they are what they are. He is the embodiment of direct, unreflecting action, the man of normal circumstances who moves through life with the free-and-easy manners of the forties, talking of future conquests of women, boasting of duels, and declaring his *droit de seigneur* over the peasants with a light heart, while the servile rabble applauds. 

And yet, if you ask me what role he truly plays, it is this: he is the living stone wall against which the tormented, hyper-conscious spirit of the underground beats itself in a fever of impotent spite. We hate him—we hate his handsome, stupid face, his abrupt self-confident voice, his witticisms which are often frightfully stupid—and yet we are drawn to him, we swallow our insults, we even make advances to him when school days are over, because his stupid, unclouded fullness of being stands as a silent reproach to our own diseased, isolated, and agonizing consciousness. He is the master of the feast, the center around whom the others gather to drink champagne and toast old times, while the underground man sits apart, ignored, drowsy, yet swelling with a dark, hysterical determination to assert himself, to thrust his unwelcome speech upon them, and to prove, through every agonizing humiliation, that he too exists, even if he must do so as a spiteful brute.

He is a clerk, an anæmic, scrofulous little man with strangely flaxen mutton-chop whiskers, soft-hearted yet conceited, who attaches himself to the cause of progress and the younger generation from enthusiasm, becoming one of those numerous and varied legion of dullards, of half-animate abortions, half-educated coxcombs who attach themselves to the idea most in fashion only to vulgarise it and caricature every cause they serve. He is one of the lodgers most respected by Amalia Ivanovna because he does not get drunk and pays regularly for his lodgings, and though he is good-natured and tries to expound the system of Fourier and the Darwinian theory, he is regarded by Pyotr Petrovitch with sarcasm and suspected of being a liar with no connections of any consequence. He is busy enlarging on his favourite subject, the foundation of a new special commune, and burning with impatience to discourse on Dounia and to offer progressive thoughts that might console Pyotr Petrovitch and promote his development, even while there is confusion between them regarding the thrashing of Katerina Ivanovna a month prior. Beyond these things, my recollection does not reach, and I cannot say what further part he plays.

Ferfitchkin plays the part of that nasty little snigger like a puppy yapping, always there to follow Zverkov and find my position exquisitely ludicrous and embarrassing, shouting out with a nasty little snigger to spare my blushes and then flying out at me, turning as red as a lobster and looking me in the face with fury when I remind him that I am dining at my own expense and not at other people's, and positively squealing at Zverkov's burlesque narratives; yes, he is one of those who make me feel so crushed and humiliated that I think, Good Heavens, these are not the people for me!

Gaganov is challenged, or rather, it is Gaganov who is furious and demanding satisfaction, while Nikolay Vsyevolodovitch Stavrogin is the one facing him across the weapons, though we see Stavrogin declining to restrict the duel even while declaring he will not fire to kill, firing into the air or near his adversary until Gaganov goes right up to the barrier. I cannot recall the precise outcome of that third exchange beyond Gaganov pressing forward to make use of his rights with the third shot while Mavriky Nikolaevitch says nothing and Kirillov oversees it all.
I cannot recall that specific sentence or its exact chapter from the recollections available to me, for my memory does not retain every phrase, and I must not invent what is not there before my mind.

I cannot recall that line, nor can I find it in the recollections before me, for my memory sometimes fails me regarding the precise placement of a phrase among the innumerable thoughts and pages that have flowed through my mind, and it is entirely possible that the sentence you ask after belongs to a part of the narrative which is not here present to my eye.

That line is to be found in the eleventh chapter of the second part. We torment ourselves so often with our own dualisms, swinging back and forth between an extreme, almost senseless confidence in our fellows and a vile, gloomy suspiciousness, while the days pass in silence and the heart accuses itself both of causing some new monstrosity and of daring to measure the silence at all.
